comparisons.evidence: P proposes "permit overbooking" and targeting a "keystone node," which relies on high-level macro-allocation systems or isolated infrastructure. Q proposes a "Curb operating system" and "Backpressure gates," which directly target the physical triggers of systemic gridlock, explicitly addressing how localized friction causes "spillback that reduces the capacity of the entire network."

P's mechanisms rely on highly speculative cross-domain behavioral leaps, such as idea #6 assuming that "peak-pricing habits transfer across domains" from utility bills to road choices. Conversely, Q outlines tight, mechanically grounded causal pathways rooted in fluid dynamics, explaining how "Controlled dwell reduces double-parking and merge turbulence, which restores junction discharge capacity."

P's solutions introduce massive institutional and regulatory hurdles, such as assuming a comprehensive, pre-existing "road-access permit" system can easily be overbooked and fined. Q provides highly viable, progressive interventions that can be piloted locally with low friction, such as a "ten-block pilot" for curb reservations or an opt-in trial "across three buildings for six weeks."

Both outputs excel at establishing concrete operational parameters and testing logic. P provides clear pre-deployment simulation criteria ("simulate removing top-1 node vs. top-10 nodes"), while Q outlines excellent physical field controls ("Alternate treated and untreated blocks for four weeks; kill or redesign the idea unless lane-obstruction minutes... fall").

Both entries exhibit outstanding creativity by importing frameworks from completely distinct fields. P uniquely maps airline yield management ("permit overbooking") and utility cross-billing to city transit, while Q beautifully adapts concepts from operating systems ("Backpressure gates") and immunology ("Hotspot immune memory").

P and Q both span highly diverse regions of the solution space. P covers permit markets, zoning incentives, parking buybacks, and utility pricing channels. Q successfully explores digital curb reservation architectures, automated dynamic turn meshes, destination-level impact budgets, and localized logistics cooperatives.

P curates a distinct, non-redundant set of 10 candidate ideas and explicitly filters them down to the strongest recommendations. Q dilutes its focus by listing 16 items that contain clear padding and conceptual near-duplicates, such as overlapping ideas for curb management (#1 "Curb operating system" and #6 "Curb compaction") and off-street queuing (#8 "Queue-neutral building code" and #16 "Block mobility lobbies").
